doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Covers, emulating black R&B and avoiding temptation
summary: The band played obscure covers, trying to emulate rather than copy, and Hunter was never tempted by producers.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Were you doing your own tunes at that early point?

A handful of them. I mean we were like a covers band doing what we thought were obscure covers. We were trying not to be complete copyists. We’d do the lesser well known things that were standard. I can’t remember what we would have done now.

Actually I think I did things that I thought nobody had covered like “Further On Up the Road” by Bobby Bland. I didn’t realize that your Claptons and whatnot had already done it to death since then, which I thought that was an indication I was a good judge of a song, because I mean I found several, a long time ago sort of there was an Ivory Joe Hunter tune called “I Need You So” and I started doing that occasionally if we were busking. And I saw it on the arse end of a compilation of his stuff, thinking it was just some obscure, and I didn’t realize it had become an R&B standard, that every vocal group used to do it. I had no idea. So I thought that I’m not a bad judge then, am I?
Did you feel compelled to try to re-create what you heard on these records as close as possible?
Less re-create than, what do you call it, there is a word for it, emulate.

Yeah, trying to get the same spirit of that and I think you can stultify something by trying to absolutely replicate it so I was trying to, I was trying to convey the same spirit. I always felt that for the most part, with a few exceptions that white America and British acts who attempted that style of music used to lose the finesse and they’d compensate by adding a bit more aggression. But the slinkiness, the sort of sinuous poetics of grace of the way the black performers used to do it I think was lost on a lot of us Caucasians. So I tried to copy that element of it. I mean sometimes people like Georgie Fame would get the groove, they’d find the groove, I mean, and Duffy Power, he was another more obscure sort of British white soul singer, and he’d add his own little thing of strangeness to it. He used to transcend that thing of copyist. He’d add his own element to it.
Were you compelled by, or suggested to by producers, like, “James if you just would do this we could sign you” or —

No. I never had that carrot dangled in front of me. I was lucky. I don’t know how resolute I would have been if I’d been faced by any sort of temptation or whatever. There was maybe a couple of instances but the promise wasn’t, you know, maybe the carrot wasn’t big enough for me to go for it.
To get up to that next level or whatever.
Yeah It didn’t seem like it was going to be an obvious next step. But I don’t really remember being tempted you know.
